analysis.one_liner: Lets workers at larger employers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 119 House sponsors, all Democrats, but never got a committee hearing or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven days) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a sick child, parent, or spouse, or to handle medical, legal, and safety needs after domestic violence or sexual assault. Employers with equally generous existing policies would be exempt, and the Labor Department would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly half of American workers who lacked any paid sick time, and especially low-wage workers: the bill's findings state that 79 percent of families in the lowest earnings quartile lacked paid sick time [S3]. It also would have covered workers who need time off to recover from or escape domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn at least one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year unless the employer offers more [S2][S3].
Covers time to care for a sick child, parent, or spouse, and for the bill's stated purposes of preventive care that catches illness early and reduces emergency care costs [S2][S3].
Allows paid leave for medical attention, counseling, relocation, or court proceedings related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking, with confidentiality protections [S2][S3].
Bars employers from firing or retaliating against workers for using the time, and gives the Labor Department investigative and enforcement authority plus a private right to sue [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, who would pay wages for up to 56 hours of sick leave per worker per year and face recordkeeping, notice-posting, and certification duties [S2][S3]. Opponents argued the mandate and litigation exposure would fall hardest on small firms and could reduce hiring or hours; the bill did not fund the benefit, so the cost is borne by the businesses subject to it.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is an unfunded employer cost: wages for up to 56 hours per employee per year plus compliance and recordkeeping, a burden that falls proportionally harder on small firms near the 15-employee threshold than on large corporations [S2][S3].
The bill creates litigation exposure and a broad private right to sue with attorney's fees, which opponents argued invites disputes over leave denials and retaliation claims [S3].

Because employers absorb the cost rather than the government, some economists argue such mandates lead to slower hiring or fewer hours for the lowest-wage workers the benefit is meant to help; the bill text itself anticipates a certification requirement for absences over three days, adding paperwork for workers and doctors [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is concrete and large: paid time to see a doctor, care for a sick child, or handle an abusive relationship without losing income or the job, which the bill's findings tie to better health and lower emergency-care costs [S3]. The main honest cost is that employers, particularly small ones, pay for the leave and compliance, with some risk of reduced hours at the margin. The bill's design softens this somewhat with a 15-employee threshold, a 56-hour cap, an exemption for employers with equivalent policies, and no cash-out on separation. Weighing a modest, arguable employment effect against guaranteed income protection for sick workers, the benefits are substantial for the population it covers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the Healthy Families Act on May 12, 2011, with 80 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Education and the Workforce, Oversight and Government Reform, and House Administration committees on the day of introduction [S1][S5].

The bill was subsequently referred to the Subcommittee on Federal Workforce, U.S. Postal Service, and Labor Policy (May 13, 2011) and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections (September 8, 2011); the action history ends there [S5].
The bill accumulated 118 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never reached the House floor [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have been required to provide paid sick leave, who avoided the mandate and its costs; workers without paid sick time gained nothing.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 118 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing or markup in the committee of primary referral; the record shows only referral to subcommittees and no further action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 118 cosponsors were Democrats [S4]; the bill died in committees of the Republican-controlled House without a hearing or vote [S5].

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These industries employ many of the low-wage workers who most often lack paid sick time, so the mandate's cost would land on them while its benefit would flow to their workers; their interest in blocking the bill ran against workers' access to paid leave [S3].
The bill's findings argue that paid sick time increases use of routine, lower-cost preventive care and reduces emergency-room visits, which would modestly shift demand toward primary care [S3].
